newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian oil workers renew strike threat.
newsitem.headline: Colombian oil workers renew strike threat.

text.p: BOGOTA, May 8 Reuter - Colombia's main oil workers' union renewed its threat to stage a nationwide work stoppage Thursday, after talks with the government broke down in total disagreement over natural gas operations.

Hernando Hernandez, head of the 7,000-strong union known by its Spanish-language acronym as USO, emerged from the talks with government officials including Interior Minister Horacio Serpa saying union leaders would now set a deadline, within a matter of hours, for the start of the potentially crippling work stoppage.
The state oil company Ecopetrol favors the creation of a separate company, jointly financed by the government and private sector, to handle gas production and distribution across Colombia.
USO is insisting that gas operations remain under the complete control of Ecopetrol, however, and argues that there should be no move to break up the state-run oil giant.
The dispute over plans to create an independent gas company, to be called Ecogas, is the main sticking point in collective contract talks that have been going on all year.

"There's been no agreement as of today," Hernandez said of the gas issue. He added that the government had vowed to continue working on a possible negotiated settlement, however, and said union leaders were prepared to return to the bargaining table at any time, whether or not a strike had already begun.

"The bottom line is that this is political problem," Hernandez told reporters. "The Ministry of Mines and Energy doesn't want Ecopetrol to have anything to do with the transportation of natural gas," he said.

Government officials could not be reached for immediate comment. But Ecopetrol officials have said in the past that the company was keen on the idea of being relieved of the burden of administering natural gas operations.
Natural gas output averaged 444 million cubic feet per day in 1996 and production is expected to rise to 517 cubic feet per day in 1997. (-- Tom Brown, Bogota newsroom, 571 610 7944)
